                      fig.height = 4.2, fig.align = "center", dpi = 110)
options(digits = 4)

```{r setup}
library(doobr)
data(itaload)
str(itaload)
```

This vignette works through the applied example of the accompanying paper on the
packaged data. The horizon is a week and the evaluation ensembles are 100 paths
per fold so that the vignette builds quickly; the paper uses a fortnight and
larger ensembles.

The reason to run the method on this series rather than a simulated one is that
here it finds things. Two of them are worth the whole vignette: a calendar
specification that *improves every score while being demonstrably wrong*, and a
conditional-scale target that improves the step-2 test by eighteen orders of
magnitude while barely moving the energy score. Neither is visible without the
martingale-difference tests.

## The series

```{r fig.height = 3.6}
plot(itaload$date, itaload$load / 1e3, type = "l", col = "grey30",
     xlab = "", ylab = "GWh", main = "Italian daily electricity load")
```

Two seasonal cycles — the weekly working-day/weekend alternation and the annual
summer/winter double peak — plus holiday troughs that sit well below any
weekend. The variance is visibly larger at both annual peaks than in the
shoulder seasons.

```{r}
y <- itaload$load
n <- length(y)
h <- 7L                                  # one week ahead
train <- seq_len(n - h)
test  <- seq.int(n - h + 1L, n)          # held back for the fan chart
mlags <- 1:14
```

## Three calendars

The calendar is deterministic and known arbitrarily far ahead, which is what the
method requires of a regressor. We try three versions of it, in increasing
order of care.

```{r}
shift <- function(x, k) {
  m <- length(x)
  if (k > 0) c(rep(0, k), head(x, m - k)) else c(tail(x, m + k), rep(0, -k))
}

dow <- model.matrix(~ dow, itaload)[, -1, drop = FALSE]
hol <- as.numeric(itaload$holiday)

X_dow  <- dow                                            # weekday only
X_hol  <- cbind(dow, hol = hol,                          # + holidays, same day
                br = as.numeric(itaload$bridge))
X_full <- cbind(X_hol,                                   # + holiday spillover
                hol_next = shift(hol, -1),
                hol_prev = shift(hol,  1))
```

```{r}
fit1 <- function(Xm) doob_fit(
  y[train], horizon = h, xreg = Xm[train, , drop = FALSE],
  mean_model_fn = lm_model_fn, mlags = mlags, predict_mean_fn = lm_predict_fn,
  nsim_eval = 100L, md_type = "additive", md_stat = "F", seed = 1, verbose = FALSE
)

f_dow  <- fit1(X_dow)
f_hol  <- fit1(X_hol)
f_full <- fit1(X_full)
```

```{r}
report <- function(...) {
  fs <- list(...)
  t(sapply(fs, function(f) {
    e <- f$oof_resid[f$bank_idx]
    c(resid_sd = sd(e),
      acf1 = acf(e, plot = FALSE, lag.max = 7)$acf[2],
      acf7 = acf(e, plot = FALSE, lag.max = 7)$acf[8],
      p_step1 = f$md$step1, p_step2 = f$md$step2,
      ES = f$eval$mean_es, VS = f$eval$mean_vs)
  }))
}
tab <- report(dow = f_dow, dow_hol = f_hol, dow_hol_spill = f_full)
rownames(tab) <- c("weekday only", "+ holiday, same day", "+ holiday spillover")
tab
```

Read the second row against the first. Adding the holiday and bridge dummies
cuts the residual standard deviation by 27% and the energy score by 14%. On any
fit or scoring criterion it is an improvement, and a large one.

The step-1 martingale-difference test says it is a disaster: the p-value falls
from 2.6e-03 to 9.5e-32, and the residual lag-1 autocorrelation jumps from
0.004 to 0.399. Something that looks like a better model has acquired a gross
violation of the property the whole method rests on.

The diagnosis is in the structure of Italian holidays. They cluster — Christmas
to Epiphany, the 25 April / 1 May pair, mid-August — and load stays depressed on
the days *around* a marked holiday, not only on the holiday itself. A same-day
indicator removes the large central drop and leaves the shoulders behind as a
run of correlated residuals. The third row allows the effect to spill one day
either side:

```{r}
tab[, c("resid_sd", "acf1", "p_step1", "ES")]
```

The lag-1 autocorrelation returns to 0.041, the step-1 p-value recovers by
twenty-four orders of magnitude, *and* the residual standard deviation falls a
further 20%. The test did not trade fit for correctness; it pointed at a
genuinely missing feature.

This is the case for testing rather than scoring. The energy score ranked the
broken calendar above the bare one. It was not wrong to do so — the broken
calendar does predict better — but a scenario generator built on it resamples
innovations that are 40% predictable from their own past, which is precisely
what must not happen.

### What is left over

```{r}
c(acf7 = tab["+ holiday spillover", "acf7"],
  p_step1 = tab["+ holiday spillover", "p_step1"])
```

The best calendar still leaves a lag-7 autocorrelation of 0.23 and a step-1
p-value of 5e-08. This is real and we have not removed it. Adding annual
harmonics, day-of-week by season interactions, a linear trend, more lags (up to
28), and heating and cooling degree days from the packaged temperature series
each leave it between 0.22 and 0.26. Whatever drives it operates at the weekly
lag and is not a smooth function of the calendar or of contemporaneous
temperature.

The practical consequence is worth stating plainly, because it is the kind of
thing a diagnostic is for: the innovation bank still contains predictable
structure at the weekly lag, so the simulated paths will understate how much a
week-ahead outcome can be anticipated. The ensembles below are usable but not
innocent, and a paper reporting them should say so.

## Step 2: the conditional scale

One thing to understand before setting the number of folds. The
conditional-scale model is trained on **out-of-fold** residuals, because
in-sample residuals are exactly what the method exists to avoid. So the step-2
training sample is the innovation bank, whose size is the number of folds times
the fold length — not the length of the series. Leave `n_folds` at its default
and the series is partitioned exhaustively:

```{r}
c(n_folds = f_full$n_folds, bank_size = length(f_full$bank),
  series = length(f_full$spec$w))
```

Cutting `n_folds` to 8 to save time would leave 49 observations to fit a
13-parameter scale model, and the fitted variances come out wild — on this
series that alone drove `c_hat` above 7. If the scale model misbehaves, check
the bank size first.

```{r}
fit2 <- function(vt) doob_fit(
  y[train], horizon = h, xreg = X_full[train, , drop = FALSE],
  mean_model_fn = lm_model_fn, mlags = mlags, predict_mean_fn = lm_predict_fn,
  variance_model_fn = lm_model_fn, vlags = c(1L, 7L),
  predict_variance_fn = lm_predict_fn, var_target = vt,
  nsim_eval = 100L, md_type = "additive", md_stat = "F", seed = 1, verbose = FALSE
)
f_sq <- fit2("squared")
f_la <- fit2("logabs")
```

```{r}
t(sapply(list(constant = f_full, squared = f_sq, logabs = f_la),
         function(f) c(c_hat = f$c_hat, kappa_hat = f$kappa_hat,
                       scale_failures = f$n_scale_failures,
                       p_step2 = f$md$step2, ES = f$eval$mean_es)))
```

Now the mirror image of the calendar story. The energy score separates the three
fits by about 1%: constant 34559, squared 35076, logabs 34185. By that measure
there is nothing to choose. The step-2 test separates them by eighteen orders of
magnitude — 2.7e-23 for the homoskedastic fit against 2.8e-05 for `logabs`. The
squared-residual target is *worse* than no scale model at all on this series
(2.0e-25).

Two mechanisms are behind that last result, and both are visible in the table.

**Least squares on squared residuals has no sign constraint.** At 67 of the 980
bank states the fitted variance lands at or below zero. Those states are
excluded from the innovation bank rather than clipped into it:

```{r}
c(failures = f_sq$n_scale_failures, of = length(f_sq$bank) + f_sq$n_scale_failures,
  sigma_floor = f_sq$sigma_range[1], sigma_ceiling = f_sq$sigma_range[2])
```

Exclusion rather than clipping matters more than it looks. `c_hat` is a
root-mean-square and is not robust; a state whose fitted variance is near zero
against an ordinary residual produces an enormous standardised residual, and a
handful of those dominate the constant. An earlier implementation clipped them
into the bank, which on this series drove `c_hat` to 8.67 and inflated the mean
energy score from 230,247 to 753,751 — a 75-fold inflation of the simulated
scale, with every diagnostic computed on the normalised bank still passing.
Winsorising the standardised residuals was tried as an alternative and is wrong:
it trims the tails of the innovation distribution, which is exactly what a
scenario generator must reproduce. The contamination comes from broken variance
estimates, not from large residuals.

**Fitting `log|e|` is positive by construction**, so `logabs` has nothing to
exclude, and it needs only `Var(log|eta|)` finite rather than a fourth moment.
The price is a multiplicative bias: least squares on `log|eps|` estimates
`log(sigma) + kappa` with `kappa = E log|eta|`, about -0.635 for Gaussian
innovations. Here:

```{r}
c(kappa_hat = f_la$kappa_hat, implied_factor = exp(f_la$kappa_hat),
  c_hat = f_la$c_hat)
```

`kappa_hat` of -0.86 is more negative than the Gaussian value, consistent with
innovations heavier-tailed than normal. Exponentiating the fit without
correction would understate the conditional standard deviation by a factor of
2.4. `c_hat` removes that without knowing the innovation distribution — and
note that it is **carried into the conditional variance**, not used to normalise
the bank. Normalising the bank alone would leave the whole scale resting on the
variance model; moving the constant across lets a multiplicative bias in the
fitted variance cancel in the product.

A caveat on reading the step-2 column at all: the second test is a statement
about `e^2 - v` given that the first step has produced genuine martingale
differences. Step 1 still rejects at 5e-08 here, so some of what step 2 sees may
be mean misspecification arriving in the squared residuals. The ranking of the
three targets is informative; the absolute p-values are not clean.

## Calibration of the simulated paths

```{r}
calibration_tests(f_la)
```

```{r fig.height = 3.4}
ct <- calibration_tests(f_la)
hist(ct$rank$ranks, breaks = 12, col = "grey85", border = "white",
     main = "Rank histogram, out-of-fold", xlab = "rank of the realisation")
```

The three blocks answer different questions, and here they disagree in an
informative way. The rank histogram rejects at 6.7e-04. The permutation test on
the energy score returns 0.93 and the band-depth test 0.90 — and a p-value near
*one* is itself a diagnosis, not a pass: it means the realised path is more
central than the simulated ones, i.e. the ensemble is too dispersed as a
trajectory. (The variogram test, at 0.56, is the one block that sees nothing
either way.) The rejection and the near-ones point the same way. The mean model leaves predictable
structure, that structure inflates the innovation bank, and the paths come out
wider than the data warrants.

Compare the bare-calendar fit, whose residual standard deviation is 70% larger:

```{r}
t(sapply(list(dow = f_dow, full = f_full, logabs = f_la), function(f) {
  k <- calibration_tests(f)
  c(p_rank = k$rank$pval, p_energy = k$perm_es$fisher_pval,
    p_band = k$band$fisher_pval)
}))
```

The over-dispersion signature is strongest exactly where the mean model is
worst. One caveat on the first column: the pooled rank test treats ranks at
adjacent steps within a fold as independent when they are positively dependent,
so it is mildly liberal — under a correctly specified model it rejects 12–14% of
the time at a nominal 5%. Read it comparatively, as above, rather than against
0.05.

## The held-back week

The future calendar is known, so it can be passed directly to `simulate()`:

```{r}
paths <- simulate(f_la, nsim = 2000L, seed = 11,
                  newxreg = X_full[test, , drop = FALSE])
paths
```

```{r}
qs  <- apply(paths$paths, 1L, quantile, c(0.05, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.95)) / 1e3
act <- y[test] / 1e3
hist_tail <- (n - h - 20L):(n - h)

plot(c(hist_tail, test), c(y[hist_tail], act) / 1e3, type = "n",
     xlab = "day index", ylab = "GWh",
     main = sprintf("%d-day fan chart, held-back week", h))
polygon(c(test, rev(test)), c(qs[1, ], rev(qs[5, ])),
        col = adjustcolor("steelblue", 0.20), border = NA)
polygon(c(test, rev(test)), c(qs[2, ], rev(qs[4, ])),
        col = adjustcolor("steelblue", 0.35), border = NA)
lines(hist_tail, y[hist_tail] / 1e3, col = "grey30")
lines(test, qs[3, ], col = "steelblue", lwd = 2)
lines(test, act, col = "firebrick", lwd = 2)
legend("topleft", bty = "n", lwd = 2, cex = 0.85,
       col = c("grey30", "steelblue", "firebrick"),
       legend = c("history", "simulated median", "realised"))
```

```{r}
pit <- rowMeans(paths$paths < y[test])
rbind(quantile_of_realisation = round(pit, 3))
```

Seven points say very little — the out-of-fold calibration tests above are the
assessment, because they average over 140 independent weeks. The fan chart is
here to be looked at, not scored.

## A scenario tree

For a multistage stochastic program the flat ensemble is replaced by a tree that
branches on the martingale component, so the Doob decomposition is inherited
node by node.

```{r}
tr <- simulate(f_la, output = "tree", seed = 12,
               branching = c(5L, 3L, rep(2L, h - 2L)),
               newxreg = X_full[test, , drop = FALSE])
tr
```

The branching is front-loaded deliberately: early uncertainty is what a
here-and-now decision must hedge, and the leaf count is the product of the
branching vector, so late stages have to be thin.

The property that makes the tree usable is that it adds no predictability of its
own. At the root the model forecast is computable directly, so the identity can
be checked against it:

```{r}
sp <- f_la$spec
w  <- tail(sp$w, max(c(sp$mlags, sp$vlags)))
yl <- setNames(w[length(w) - sp$mlags + 1L], paste0("lag", sp$mlags))
mu <- as.numeric(sp$predict_mean_fn(f_la$models$mean, yl,
                                    X_full[test, , drop = FALSE][1L, , drop = FALSE]))

ch <- tr$nodes[tr$nodes$stage == 1L, ]
c(tree_mean = sum(ch$cond_prob * ch$value_model), model_forecast = mu,
  abs_error = abs(sum(ch$cond_prob * ch$value_model) - mu))
```

Deeper in the tree the conditional scale differs from node to node, but the
*atoms* do not: the quantised innovation bank is shared by every node at a given
stage. So the standardised child deviations must coincide across all parents,
which is checkable without knowing any node's conditional variance:

```{r}
d   <- tr$nodes[tr$nodes$stage == 2L, ]
pat <- sapply(split(d, d$parent), function(k) {
  dev <- k$value_model - sum(k$cond_prob * k$value_model)
  dev / sqrt(sum(k$cond_prob * dev^2))
})
round(pat, 12)
max(apply(pat, 1L, function(r) diff(range(r))))
```

Identical to machine precision across the five stage-2 parents. The node-by-node
verification of both moment identities, at every stage and under both the levels
and the differenced recursion, is in the package's test suite.

## Why temperature is not in the model

The packaged data includes a `temperature` column, and it is tempting to use it.
It does help:

```{r}
X_temp <- cbind(X_full,
                hdd = pmax(18 - itaload$temperature, 0),
                cdd = pmax(itaload$temperature - 21, 0))
f_temp <- fit1(X_temp)

t(sapply(list(no_temp = f_full, with_temp = f_temp),
         function(f) c(resid_sd = sd(f$oof_resid[f$bank_idx]),
                       p_step1 = f$md$step1, ES = f$eval$mean_es)))
```

The energy score improves by 7% and the residual standard deviation by 3%. The
step-1 p-value does not improve, which is the third appearance of the same
lesson in this vignette: a better score is not a better specification.

The deeper problem is not statistical. Those scores are the scores of
simulations made *given a known temperature path*, because the evaluation folds
supply the realised temperature. To simulate a genuine future you must pass
`newxreg`, which means supplying a temperature path you do not have. What comes
out is then the conditional law of load given that path, not the predictive law
of load. The two differ by the variance contributed by temperature uncertainty,
which for a week-ahead electricity forecast is not small.

There are three honest responses. Use only deterministic regressors, as the main
example does, and accept a wider but correct ensemble. Condition deliberately on
a named temperature scenario and report it as such, which is legitimate for
stress testing. Or model load and temperature jointly — the multivariate
extension, which is the right answer and is not yet implemented. A single-
equation method cannot resolve this, and a regressor whose future is unknown
will always flatter the diagnostics while producing ensembles that are too
narrow in use.

## Summary

```{r}
t(sapply(list(bare = f_dow, broken_calendar = f_hol, good_calendar = f_full,
              squared = f_sq, logabs = f_la),
         function(f) c(resid_sd = sd(f$oof_resid[f$bank_idx]),
                       c_hat = f$c_hat, failures = f$n_scale_failures,
                       p_step1 = f$md$step1, p_step2 = f$md$step2,
                       ES = f$eval$mean_es)))
```

Four things to carry away from this series.

A specification can improve every score while becoming grossly misspecified for
simulation; only a test on the first estimation step catches it. The second step
needs its own test, because the energy score separates conditional-scale targets
by 1% where the test separates them by eighteen orders of magnitude. The
`logabs` target avoids the sign problem of fitting squared residuals, at the cost
of a constant that must be estimated and carried into the variance rather than
discarded. And a regressor is usable here only if its future path is genuinely
known — which, for weather, it is not.
